The inverse design method uses the Reynolds Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations with the actuator disk model to simulate the effect of the turbine rotor without resolving the blade geometry.
The Trust-Region-Reflective (TRF) method is used as the optimization algorithm in the inverse design procedure.
The inverse design method is demonstrated for both conventional single-rotor horizontal axis wind turbines and multi-rotor, specifically dual-rotor wind turbines.
Manufacturing and transportation constraints on the blade geometry, such as limiting the chord between 0.01R and 0.2R, can be imposed in the inverse design process.
The mesh sensitivity study shows that a grid resolution of 101x229 cells is sufficient to obtain grid-independent results for the RANS/ADM solver.

The inverse design method prescribes the desired distributions of angle of attack and axial induction factor, rather than lift coefficient, to avoid issues with the multi-valued nature of the angle of attack-lift coefficient relationship.

The TRF method is found to be more stable and better handle constraints on the blade geometry compared to the multi-dimensional Newton iteration method, although the Newton method converges faster for unconstrained optimization problems.
The inverse design methodology is general enough to work for turbines with arbitrary number of rotor disks, and is not limited to dual-rotor wind turbines.
The RANS/ADM approach used in the inverse design method can better simulate turbulent wake mixing effects compared to potential flow methods like BEM or VLM.
The inverse design algorithm iteratively updates the blade geometry (twist and chord distributions) to minimize the difference between the calculated and desired aerodynamic performance.
An initial guess of the blade geometry is provided to the inverse design algorithm, which then converges to the final blade design that satisfies the prescribed aerodynamic performance targets.
The inverse design method is verified for three different test cases involving single-rotor wind turbines with different airfoil selections and prescribed aerodynamic performance targets.
The inverse design method is able to reproduce the original blade geometry when the desired aerodynamic performance is prescribed using either the RANS/ADM or the BEM method.
The Jacobian matrix, which represents the sensitivity of the aerodynamic performance to changes in the blade geometry, is calculated using a forward finite difference approach.

The inverse design algorithm stops when any of the following criteria are met: maximum number of iterations, minimum value of the target function, minimum change in the independent variables, or minimum norm of the gradient of the target function.
